title: When the Hymn Breaks
premise: Ines Thornbury, a meticulous property surveyor, arrives in the dying village of Hollowmere to appraise Wrenfield House, a manor whose measurements refuse to stay recorded. The village's church bell, melted down in 1911 after it was blamed for three drownings, begins ringing again at dusk, and only Ines can hear the hymn it sings—a song that rewrites the memories of anyone who hums along. As villagers who once ignored them begin to remember Ines into the village's history, Ines uncovers that the bell's last verse was never sung: it is an unfinished bargain, and the village has been feeding it names for a century. To end it, Ines must transcribe the final verse without singing it, choosing between erasing their own documented existence or letting the bell finish its song—and take the village with it.
about_author: Isandro Crane is the pen name of a former archivist who spent nine years cataloguing condemned buildings across northern England before turning to fiction. They write horror about paperwork, place, and the things that outlast both, and they still keep a surveyor's notebook by their bed.

chapters.title: The Survey Begins
chapters.summary: Ines Thornbury arrives in Hollowmere to appraise Wrenfield House, photographing every room and logging every anomaly. The house feels attentive. POV: Ines. Beat: quiet unease beneath professional routine.

chapters.title: Measurements That Move
chapters.summary: Ines remeasures the east corridor twice; the numbers differ each time. They document it, telling themselves it's settling foundations. POV: Ines. Beat: rationality straining against evidence.

chapters.title: The Village Without a Bell
chapters.summary: Ines visits St. Aldric's church, finds an empty tower and a plaque noting the bell was melted down in 1911. The vicar, Mr. Ellery, watches them too long. POV: Ines. Beat: first brush with the village's curated silence.

chapters.title: Dusk, and Ringing
chapters.summary: At dusk a bell tolls from the empty tower. No one else on the lane reacts. Ines records the sound on their phone; playback holds only wind. POV: Ines. Beat: the moment documentation fails.

chapters.title: The Drowned Choir
chapters.summary: In the parish archive Ines finds a 1911 newspaper clipping: three choirboys drowned the night the bell last rang; the village voted to melt it. One name is scratched out. POV: Ines. Beat: history revealing a wound kept deliberately closed.

chapters.title: Mrs. Halloway Remembers Me
chapters.summary: Shopkeeper Mrs. Halloway greets Ines by name and recalls a childhood visit Ines never made. Her memory is warm, specific, wrong. POV: Ines. Beat: the horror of being written into someone else's past.

chapters.title: The House Appraises Back
chapters.summary: Wrenfield House responds to Ines's inventory: rooms appear on their floor plan that they never drew, furnished, lived-in. A child's coat hangs in one. POV: Ines. Beat: the survey becomes a conversation.

chapters.title: Ellery's Warning
chapters.summary: Vicar Ellery tells Ines to leave before the bell learns their voice. He speaks of 'the verse' and refuses to say more. POV: Ines. Beat: ally or gatekeeper—trust uncertain.

chapters.title: Hymnal Fragment
chapters.summary: Ines finds a burned hymnal in the house's chimney flue; one page survives, lyrics ending mid-line. When read aloud, the room grows colder. POV: Ines. Beat: the song has a shape, and it wants completing.

chapters.title: The First Verse
chapters.summary: That night Ines dreams the first verse and wakes humming it. Their own notebook now contains entries in their handwriting they don't remember making. POV: Ines. Beat: contamination—the song writes back.

chapters.title: Tamsin Lowe
chapters.summary: A young woman, Tamsin, admits she hears the bell too; her grandmother vanished in 1974 after 'singing along.' She begs Ines to help her understand it. POV: Ines. Beat: reluctant alliance formed.

chapters.title: The Melted Metal
chapters.summary: Records show the bell's bronze was recast into a war memorial and three door knockers around the village. The bell was never destroyed—only distributed. POV: Ines. Beat: the enemy is everywhere and ordinary.

chapters.title: Names in the Ledger
chapters.summary: Ines discovers a ledger in the vestry listing names and dates spanning 1911 to the present, each entry annotated 'verse owed.' New ink appears: their own name. POV: Ines. Beat: time is running out, literally inscribed.

chapters.title: Memory of a House
chapters.summary: Wrenfield House shows Ines a vision through its floorboards: the night in 1911 when the sexton rang the bell deliberately, trading his sons' lives for the village's prosperity. POV: Ines (vision). Beat: the origin sin revealed.

chapters.title: The Prosperous Decade
chapters.summary: Ines cross-references harvest records: every year following a 'verse owed' entry, Hollowmere flourished unnaturally. The village has been paying in people. POV: Ines. Beat: complicity of the whole community.

chapters.title: Ellery Confesses
chapters.summary: Ellery admits the vicars have always been the bell's bookkeepers, maintaining the ledger so the singing stays 'managed.' He is tired. He wants it to end but fears the cost. POV: Ines. Beat: loyalty vs. truth crystallizes in him.

chapters.title: Tamsin Sings
chapters.summary: Against warnings, Tamsin hums the second verse to feel close to her lost grandmother. By morning she cannot remember her own mother's face. POV: Ines. Beat: grief weaponized; the price made personal.

chapters.title: What the Song Takes
chapters.summary: Ines maps the pattern: the bell doesn't kill—it edits. Each singer loses memories, which become the bell's verses. The song is built entirely of stolen remembering. POV: Ines. Beat: theme of memory made monstrous.

chapters.title: The Scratched Name
chapters.summary: Ines identifies the scratched-out name from the 1911 clipping: the sexton himself, who vanished after ringing it. Or did he? His signature matches handwriting in Ines's own contaminated notebook. POV: Ines. Beat: dread of inherited patterns.

chapters.title: The Village Turns
chapters.summary: Villagers, sensing the ledger changing, confront Ines at Wrenfield House—not hostile, worse: welcoming, insisting Ines has 'always belonged.' POV: Ines. Beat: belonging as threat; invisibility revoked.

chapters.title: Locked In
chapters.summary: The roads out of Hollowmere loop back on themselves. Phone signals die. Ines realizes the appraisal was never a job—the house requested them by name. POV: Ines. Beat: trap closes; no exit.

chapters.title: The Third Verse
chapters.summary: The bell rings at noon instead of dusk, breaking its own pattern. Ines transcribes the third verse from the air itself, hands shaking, refusing to voice it. POV: Ines. Beat: discipline against compulsion.

chapters.title: Mrs. Halloway's Empty Chair
chapters.summary: Mrs. Halloway is gone—shop open, tea warm, every villager certain she 'moved away years ago.' Only Ines and Tamsin recall her. POV: Ines. Beat: erasure witnessed firsthand; stakes undeniable.

chapters.title: The Sexton's Room
chapters.summary: Behind Wrenfield's false wall, Ines finds the sexton's preserved study: research into the bell's casting, and a half-finished attempt to write a counter-verse. He got close. He failed. POV: Ines. Beat: hope with a corpse attached.

chapters.title: Loyalty of the Living
chapters.summary: Tamsin, losing more memories daily, asks Ines to promise that if she forgets everything, Ines will remember for her. Ines promises, hating how much it costs. POV: Ines. Beat: love as archive; loyalty vs. self-preservation.

chapters.title: Ellery's Last Entry
chapters.summary: Ellery adds his own name to the ledger voluntarily, buying the village one more good year, and leaves Ines the vestry key and one sentence: 'The last verse isn't sung. It's returned.' POV: Ines. Beat: sacrifice reframes the rules.

chapters.title: Returned How
chapters.summary: Ines deciphers the sexton's notes: the bell's power came from a theft—it was cast with bronze stolen from a funeral pyre, metal that carried voices. Every verse must be given back, not silenced. POV: Ines. Beat: solution takes shape.

chapters.title: The Bell's Voice
chapters.summary: At midnight the bell speaks through the house's pipes in a chorus of stolen voices—including Mrs. Halloway's, and, newly, Ellery's. It offers Ines anything, if they'll just sing. POV: Ines. Beat: temptation peaks.

chapters.title: The Offer
chapters.summary: The bell shows Ines a life where they were never invisible: parents who remembered them, colleagues who loved them. All they must do is complete the hymn. POV: Ines. Beat: deepest wound exploited.

chapters.title: Refusal
chapters.summary: Ines burns their contaminated notebook pages one by one, keeping only original observations, and answers the bell with silence. The house groans like something denied. POV: Ines. Beat: resolve forged in loss.

chapters.title: Tamsin Forgets Ines
chapters.summary: Tamsin looks at Ines with polite blankness. Ines keeps the promise anyway, reading their shared days aloud to her from notes, rebuilding her memory by hand each morning. POV: Ines. Beat: heartbreak; documentation as devotion.

chapters.title: The Gathering Verse
chapters.summary: The bell begins ringing continuously. Villagers drift toward the churchyard, humming, faces serene. Ines has until the hymn reaches the fourth verse's end. POV: Ines. Beat: clock running down.

chapters.title: Into the Tower
chapters.summary: Ines climbs the empty bell tower carrying the sexton's notes, the surviving hymnal page, and the ledger. The air up there is thick with waiting voices. POV: Ines. Beat: ascent toward confrontation.

chapters.title: The Unmade Bell
chapters.summary: In the tower's emptiness, the bell exists anyway—vast, molten-edged, assembled from every knocker and memorial ingot across the village, humming itself toward completion. POV: Ines. Beat: the antagonist fully revealed.

chapters.title: The Bargain Offered
chapters.summary: The bell offers a trade: Ines's entire remembered life for the village's release. Ines sees the trap—memories are what the bell eats; surrendering them feeds it forever. POV: Ines. Beat: seeing through the final lie.

chapters.title: The Last Verse Returned
chapters.summary: Ines does not sing. Instead they read aloud—every name in the ledger, every stolen memory they've documented, giving each voice back its words without joining the melody. The bell cracks note by note. POV: Ines. Beat: climax; documentation becomes exorcism.

chapters.title: Silence, Then Birds
chapters.summary: The bell shatters into dead bronze. The villagers wake in the churchyard weeping, remembering everyone they lost, including Mrs. Halloway, who walks out of the mist holding her shop keys. POV: Ines. Beat: release and grief entwined.

chapters.title: The Final Appraisal
chapters.summary: Ines completes the survey honestly: Wrenfield House, structurally unsound, recommended for demolition. The house lets them. On the last page, where anomalies were logged, Ines writes only: 'It let go.' POV: Ines. Beat: professional closure as emotional closure.

chapters.title: What Ines Kept
chapters.summary: Leaving Hollowmere, Ines passes Tamsin, who remembers nothing of them—but presses a scrap of paper into their hand: her own handwriting, 'Thank you,' written nightly on instruction she can't recall. POV: Ines. Beat: bittersweet proof the promise held.

chapters.title: Coda: The Notebook
chapters.summary: Weeks later, Ines files the report and keeps one private notebook: every name returned, every memory restored, dated and signed. Documentation was always a kind of prayer—and this once, something answered. POV: Ines. Beat: resolution; memory honored, silence chosen freely.
